lessons.title: Grammar: Present simple vs present continuous

items.definition: choosing between routines and actions happening right now
items.explanationTR:
Use the present simple for routines, facts and permanent situations at work: things that happen regularly or that are generally true.
• Form: base verb, adding -s/-es for he/she/it: 'The department opens at nine.' / 'She manages a small team.'
• Common time words: usually, every day, on Mondays, often, always.

Use the present continuous for actions happening right now, or temporary situations around the present moment.
• Form: am/is/are + verb-ing: 'He is finishing some paperwork at the moment.' / 'We are hiring three new interns this month.'
• Common time words: now, at the moment, currently, this week, these days.

Compare:
• 'She works in the finance department.' (a fact about her job)
• 'She is working from home this week.' (a temporary situation)
• 'The team meets every Monday.' (a routine)
• 'The team is meeting right now.' (happening at this moment)

Some verbs, such as know, believe and want, are rarely used in the continuous form, even when they describe something true right now.

questions.prompt: Our department ---- reports every Friday afternoon.
questions.explanationTR: The routine described by 'every Friday afternoon' calls for the present simple, and 'department' takes the -s form: submits. 'Is submitting' would describe a single action happening right now, not a weekly routine.

questions.prompt: Right now, the new intern ---- the filing system.
questions.explanationTR: 'Right now' points to an action in progress at this exact moment, so the present continuous is needed: is learning. 'Learns' would describe a routine rather than something happening now.

questions.prompt: My supervisor usually ---- our progress on Monday mornings.
questions.explanationTR: 'Usually' and 'on Monday mornings' describe a routine, so the present simple fits, and 'supervisor' needs the -s form: checks. 'Is checking' would wrongly suggest a single action happening now.

questions.prompt: Look! The new receptionist ---- everyone at the front desk.
questions.explanationTR: 'Look!' shows the action is happening at this exact moment, so the present continuous is correct: is greeting. 'Greets' would describe a general habit rather than what we can see now.

questions.prompt: The HR department ---- interviews every Tuesday and Thursday.
questions.explanationTR: The fixed schedule 'every Tuesday and Thursday' is a routine, so the present simple with the -s form is correct: holds. 'Is holding' would wrongly suggest one ongoing action, and 'hold' does not agree with the singular subject 'department'.

questions.prompt: I can't talk now — I ---- some paperwork for my supervisor.
questions.explanationTR: 'Now' shows the action is happening at the moment of speaking, so the present continuous with 'I am' fits: am preparing. 'Prepare' would describe a habit instead of what is happening right now.

questions.prompt: This month, the company ---- more freelancers than usual because of the busy season.
questions.explanationTR: 'This month' describes a temporary situation around now, so the present continuous is correct: is hiring. 'Hires' would describe a permanent habit rather than a change limited to this month, and 'hiring' alone is missing the verb 'is'.

questions.prompt: This month, while the office is closed for repairs, most employees ---- from home.
questions.explanationTR: 'This month' and the office being closed describe a temporary situation, so the present continuous with the plural subject is correct: are working. 'Work' would present working from home as a permanent arrangement, and 'is working' does not agree with 'employees'.

items.definition: A short article about a technology company and seven questions

passage.title: A Day at Bright Path Solutions
passage.body:
Bright Path Solutions is a technology company with its headquarters in Toronto and branches in three other cities. The company has about four hundred employees, and its human resources department hires new staff every month, including interns and freelancers who help during busy periods.

Most employees work a standard eight-hour shift, but the sales department often works overtime near the end of each quarter. Many people arrange flexible hours so they can start earlier and avoid a long commute during rush hour. Managers say that punctual employees who arrive on time set a good example for the rest of the team.

New hires spend their first three months on probation, during which the onboarding program introduces them to their supervisor, their colleagues and the tools they will need at their workstation. Employees are also encouraged to visit the break room, where people from different departments often meet and share ideas over coffee.

Teamwork is central to the company culture. Rather than working alone, employees are taught to delegate parts of a big project so that the workload is shared fairly. A receptionist welcomes visitors at the front desk, and each employee has a clear job title that describes their main responsibility.

Twice a year, every employee has a performance review with their supervisor to discuss recent achievements and plans for the future. Hard-working, efficient staff members are often considered for promotion within their department. Many employees say that Bright Path Solutions has helped them build a long and satisfying career, and new interns often stay on as full members of the team once their probation ends.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, where is Bright Path Solutions' headquarters located?
questions.explanationTR: The passage states that Bright Path Solutions has its headquarters in Toronto and branches in three other cities. The other cities are never mentioned by name in the text.

questions.prompt: In the passage, the onboarding program mainly involves ----.
options: introducing new employees to the company
a formal meeting to review an employee's performance
a shared break room for staff
questions.explanationTR: The passage describes the onboarding program introducing new hires to their supervisor, colleagues and workstation, which matches introducing new employees to the company. Overtime pay, a performance review, time off and the break room are separate ideas mentioned elsewhere in the passage.

questions.prompt: How long is the probation period for new hires at Bright Path Solutions?
questions.explanationTR: The passage says new hires spend their first three months on probation. None of the other time periods are mentioned in the text.

questions.prompt: Why do many employees arrange flexible hours?
options: to spend more time in the break room
to qualify for a faster promotion
questions.explanationTR: The passage says employees arrange flexible hours so they can start earlier and avoid a long commute during rush hour. Overtime pay, the break room, promotion and workload are mentioned elsewhere in the passage but not as the reason for flexible hours.

questions.prompt: Who welcomes visitors at the front desk?
questions.explanationTR: The passage clearly states that a receptionist welcomes visitors at the front desk. The other roles appear in the passage but are not connected to greeting visitors.

questions.prompt: How often does each employee have a performance review?
questions.explanationTR: The passage states that every employee has a performance review with their supervisor twice a year. None of the other frequencies are supported by the text.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the company make sure the workload is shared fairly on a big project?
options: by encouraging employees to delegate tasks
by asking employees to work overtime
by giving every employee a formal performance review each year
questions.explanationTR: The passage says employees are taught to delegate parts of a big project so the workload is shared fairly. Freelancers, overtime, onboarding and performance reviews are mentioned elsewhere but are not the method described for sharing workload.

lessons.title: Grammar: Modals for suggestions and opinions

items.definition: using modal verbs to suggest actions and share opinions politely
items.explanationTR:
Use modal verbs to make suggestions and share opinions politely in a meeting.
• 'Should' + base verb gives an opinion or a mild suggestion: 'We should postpone the vote.' Never add 'to' after should.
• 'Ought to' + base verb works the same way: 'You ought to mention that concern.' 'Ought' always needs 'to' before the verb.
• 'How about' and 'What about' are followed by the -ing form: 'How about delaying the decision?'
• 'Why don't we' is followed by the base verb: 'Why don't we take a short break?'
• 'Let's' + base verb makes a direct suggestion: 'Let's wrap up this item.'
• To give an opinion about something in the past that didn't happen, use 'should have' + past participle: 'We should have rescheduled sooner.'
• The negative of should is formed by adding 'not' right after it: 'You shouldn't interrupt the speaker.'

Softer modals like 'could' and 'might' often sound more polite than 'should' when your opinion is different from someone else's, since they present an idea as one option rather than a strong recommendation.

questions.prompt: We should ---- the vote until everyone has spoken.
questions.explanationTR: After the modal 'should', the verb stays in its base form: postpone. Forms like postponing, postponed, to postpone and postpones cannot follow a modal verb directly.

questions.prompt: You ought ---- mention that concern during the meeting.
questions.explanationTR: 'Ought' is always followed by 'to' before the base verb: ought to mention. None of the other words are used after 'ought'.

questions.prompt: How about ---- the decision until we have more information?
questions.explanationTR: 'How about' is followed by the -ing form of the verb: delaying. 'Delay', 'delayed', 'delays' and 'to delay' cannot follow 'how about'.

questions.prompt: Why don't we ---- a quick vote on the proposal?
questions.explanationTR: After 'why don't we', the verb takes its base form: take. 'Taking', 'took', 'to take' and 'takes' are not correct in this structure.

questions.prompt: We could ---- the meeting to next week if nobody objects.
questions.explanationTR: After the modal 'could', the verb stays in its base form: move. 'Moving', 'moved', 'to move' and 'moves' cannot follow a modal verb directly.

questions.prompt: Looking back, we ---- postponed the meeting when half the team was traveling.
questions.explanationTR: To give an opinion about a past action that didn't happen, we use 'should have' + past participle: should have postponed. 'Should' alone, 'should had', 'should has' and 'must have to' are not correct forms.

questions.prompt: You ---- interrupt the speaker; wait until she finishes her point.
questions.explanationTR: The negative of 'should' is formed by adding 'not' directly after it: shouldn't. 'Don't should', 'not should', 'shouldn't to' and 'aren't should' are not grammatical negative forms.

questions.prompt: ---- wrap up this item and move on to the next one.
questions.explanationTR: The standard suggestion form is 'Let's' + base verb: Let's wrap up. 'Let' alone is missing 'us', 'Lets' is not a suggestion form, 'Let us to' wrongly adds 'to', and 'Letting' is a gerund, not a suggestion.

items.definition: Seven short dialogues from business meetings, each missing one line

questions.prompt:
A: We're already ten minutes over. Should we cut the discussion short?
B: ----
A: Good idea, let's do that.
options: Why don't we wrap up and finish the rest by email?
I already sent the minutes to everyone yesterday afternoon.
The agenda has twelve items on it today.
He was the meeting facilitator last week.
Let's brainstorm for another hour instead.
questions.explanationTR: Only this reply directly answers the suggestion to cut the discussion short, and A's response 'Good idea, let's do that' confirms it. The other replies mention unrelated meeting details or suggest doing the opposite of shortening the discussion.

questions.prompt:
A: Sorry I'm late — did I miss much?
B: ----
A: No problem, thanks for the recap.
options: The kickoff meeting is scheduled for next Monday.
Not really, we just reviewed the agenda and assigned two action items.
Let's touch base again after lunch.
We need to reschedule the whole meeting.
questions.explanationTR: A thanks B for 'the recap', so B's line must be a short summary of what happened so far, which only this option provides. The other replies are unrelated statements about a different meeting, an invitation or a suggestion, not a recap.

questions.prompt:
A: I'd like to bring up something before we finish.
B: Sure, go ahead.
A: ----
options: The minutes from last week are ready.
I think we should reconsider the schedule for the product launch.
questions.explanationTR: A said they wanted to bring up something, so A's next line should introduce that topic, which only this option does. The other lines either close the meeting, state an unrelated fact, or make small talk instead of raising the point A mentioned.

questions.prompt:
A: What's your honest opinion about the new proposal?
B: ----
A: That's a fair point. Let's discuss it further.
options: The meeting starts at nine sharp.
She is the facilitator for today's session.
In my opinion, we should test it with a smaller group first.
Don't forget to RSVP by tomorrow.
questions.explanationTR: A asks for an opinion about the proposal, and A's next line calls it 'a fair point', so B must actually give an opinion, which only this option does. The other replies are factual statements about timing or attendance, not an opinion on the proposal.

questions.prompt:
A: We can't agree on a solution. What should we do?
B: ----
A: Good idea. Let's try that.
options: He confirmed his attendance this morning.
The agenda only has three items left.
The room is already reserved until noon.
Why don't we take a short break and come back with fresh ideas?
questions.explanationTR: A asks what the group should do about the disagreement, and only this reply offers an actual suggestion, matching A's response 'Good idea, let's try that'. The other options are unrelated facts, not suggestions.

questions.prompt:
A: Can we circle back to the staffing question later?
B: ----
A: Perfect, thanks.
options: Of course, let's revisit it after the break.
The agenda was sent this morning.
questions.explanationTR: A asks to return to a topic later, and only this reply agrees to that request, which matches A's grateful response 'Perfect, thanks'. The other options are unrelated statements that do not respond to the request to circle back.

questions.prompt:
A: Before we close, does anyone have an objection to the plan?
B: ----
A: Great, then it's settled.
options: I'll send the recap by email.
No objection from me — I think it sounds reasonable.
Let's schedule a briefing for tomorrow.
I couldn't attend the last session.
questions.explanationTR: A directly asks whether anyone objects to the plan, and A's response 'Great, then it's settled' shows the answer confirmed agreement, which only this option does. The other replies are unrelated statements that do not address the question about objections.

items.definition: the part of your email account where new messages arrive

items.definition: a file, such as a document or photo, that is sent together with an email

items.definition: to reply to a letter, email, or question

items.definition: a request for information

exampleSentences: Use a formal tone when you write to someone you do not know well.

lessons.title: Grammar: Polite requests and indirect questions

items.definition: how to make requests and ask questions more politely in business emails
items.explanationTR:
In business emails, direct questions and commands can sound demanding. Polite requests and indirect questions soften the tone.

• Common polite requests use a modal plus a softener:
  - Could you send me the file by Friday?
  - Would you mind checking this again?
  - I would appreciate it if you could confirm the date.

• Indirect questions hide a normal question inside a longer sentence. After the connecting word (if, whether, when, why, what), the word order returns to statement order — subject before verb — and we drop 'do/does/did':
  - Direct: When is the report due?
  - Indirect: Could you tell me when the report is due?
  - Direct: Did you receive my message?
  - Indirect: I was wondering if you received my message.

• Useful openers: 'I was wondering if...', 'Could you tell me...', 'Do you know whether...', 'I'd like to know if...'

These forms make an email sound professional and considerate, especially when writing to people you do not know well or when asking for something that takes their time.

questions.prompt: I was wondering ---- the shipment will arrive.
questions.explanationTR: An indirect question keeps normal statement order, so 'when' alone connects the two clauses correctly: 'I was wondering when the shipment will arrive.' 'When will' repeats direct-question order, which is wrong inside an indirect question.

questions.prompt: Could you tell me ---- the invoice was sent?
questions.explanationTR: 'If' introduces an indirect yes/no question with normal statement order: 'Could you tell me if the invoice was sent?' 'Whether does' wrongly adds an extra auxiliary, and 'that if' incorrectly combines two connectors.

questions.prompt: ---- you mind forwarding me last week's report?
questions.explanationTR: 'Would you mind' is the fixed polite pattern for asking someone to do something. 'Will/Should/Must/Have you mind' are not natural English in this request.

questions.prompt: I would appreciate it ---- you could confirm receipt of this email.
questions.explanationTR: 'I would appreciate it if...' is the standard polite fixed phrase for a request. 'That', 'whether', and 'because' do not fit this fixed expression, and 'when' changes the meaning to a time reference.

questions.prompt: She was wondering ---- the new schedule had been sent to everyone.
questions.explanationTR: 'Whether' introduces the indirect question with normal statement order: 'whether the new schedule had been sent'. The other options add an extra auxiliary or connector that does not belong in an indirect question.

questions.prompt: Which sentence is the most polite way to ask for a document?
options: Could you please send me the file when you have a moment?
You must send the file immediately.
questions.explanationTR: The polite modal 'could' plus 'please' and the softener 'when you have a moment' make this the most courteous option. The other sentences are direct commands or statements of want, which sound demanding in a business email.

questions.prompt: Do you know ---- the manager wants to move the call?
questions.explanationTR: 'Why' connects the indirect question with normal statement order: 'why the manager wants to move the call'. The other options add an unnecessary or misplaced auxiliary verb.

questions.prompt: I'd like to know ---- you have received my earlier email.
questions.explanationTR: 'If' alone correctly introduces the indirect question in statement order. The other options add an extra auxiliary ('did', 'does') or an unnecessary connector ('that'), which is not allowed in an indirect question.

items.definition: Eight short excerpts from business emails, each missing one key word

questions.prompt: I am writing with an ---- about your new pricing plans.
questions.explanationTR: After the article 'an', a singular noun is needed, so 'inquiry' fits. 'Inquiries' is plural, 'inquiring' and 'inquire' are verb forms, and 'inquest' is a different word meaning a legal investigation into a death.

questions.prompt: Please find ---- the signed contract for your records.
questions.explanationTR: 'Please find enclosed' is the standard fixed phrase for attaching a document to a letter or email. 'Enclose' and 'enclosing' are the wrong verb forms, 'enclosure' is a noun, and 'closed' is the wrong word entirely.

questions.prompt: Please accept my sincere ---- for the delay.
questions.explanationTR: After 'my sincere', a noun is needed, and 'apology' is the noun form. 'Apologize/apologized/apologizing' are verb forms, and 'apologetic' is an adjective, so none of them can follow 'my sincere'.

questions.prompt: Please mark your email as ---- if you need a reply today.
questions.explanationTR: After 'mark ... as', an adjective describes the noun, so 'urgent' is correct. 'Urgently' is an adverb, 'urgency' is a noun, and 'urge'/'urging' are verb forms, so none of them fit this position.

questions.prompt: Thank you for your ---- reply; it really helped us plan ahead.
questions.explanationTR: An adjective is needed before the noun 'reply', and 'prompt' is the adjective form. 'Promptly' is an adverb, 'promptness' is a noun, and 'prompts'/'prompted' are verb forms, so they cannot modify 'reply'.

questions.prompt: Could you ---- receipt of this email so I know it arrived?
questions.explanationTR: After the modal 'could', a verb must be in its base form, so 'acknowledge' is correct. The other options are a gerund, a past tense, a noun, and a third-person form, none of which can follow a modal verb.

questions.prompt: If the problem is not solved by Friday, I will have to ---- it to the regional manager.
questions.explanationTR: After 'have to', a verb must be in its base form, so 'escalate' (pass the problem to someone with more authority) is correct. 'Escalation' is a noun, and 'escalating', 'escalated' and 'escalates' are verb forms that cannot follow 'have to'.

questions.prompt: Sorry for the confusion — let me ---- what I meant in my last message.
questions.explanationTR: After 'let me', a verb must be in its base form, so 'clarify' is correct. 'Clarifying' and 'clarified' are wrong verb forms in this position, 'clarity' is a noun, and 'clarifies' is a third-person form.

lessons.title: Grammar: Comparatives and superlatives for trends

items.definition: how to compare numbers and describe trends using comparative and superlative forms
items.explanationTR:
When we describe charts and trends in a presentation, we often compare numbers using comparative and superlative forms.

• Comparatives (for two things or two points in time) usually add '-er' to short adjectives or use 'more' with longer ones:
  - This quarter's numbers are higher than last quarter's.
  - The new product line grew more quickly than the old one.
  - Sales in the north are lower than sales in the south.

• Superlatives (for three or more things, or the most extreme point) add '-est' or use 'most':
  - March was the busiest month of the year.
  - This is the most significant change we have seen so far.
  - The smallest increase was in the second quarter.

• Useful patterns for trends: 'a sharper increase than', 'the steadiest growth', 'far more dramatic than', 'by far the highest'.

Using comparatives and superlatives correctly helps an audience understand exactly how one number relates to another, instead of just seeing that numbers went up or down.

questions.prompt: This year's growth was ---- than last year's.
questions.explanationTR: Comparing two years needs the comparative 'faster'. 'Fastest' is a superlative, wrong for comparing just two things, and 'more fast'/'most fast' are wrong forms since 'fast' takes '-er/-est', not 'more/most'.

questions.prompt: Of all four regions, the north had ---- sales growth.
questions.explanationTR: 'Of all four regions' signals a comparison among more than two, so the superlative 'the highest' is needed. 'Higher'/'the higher' are comparatives, which only compare two things, and 'more high' is not a correct form of 'high'.

questions.prompt: The second quarter was ---- than the first.
questions.explanationTR: Comparing two quarters with 'than' needs the comparative 'stronger'. 'Strongest' is a superlative, and 'more strong'/'most strong' are wrong forms since 'strong' takes '-er/-est'.

questions.prompt: This is ---- increase we have recorded in five years.
questions.explanationTR: 'In five years' points to a comparison among many results, so the superlative 'the biggest' is correct. 'Bigger'/'the bigger' are comparatives for two items only, and 'more big' is not a correct form.

questions.prompt: The new dashboard is ---- to read than the old spreadsheet.
questions.explanationTR: 'Easy' is a two-syllable adjective ending in 'y', so its comparative is 'easier', not 'more easy'. 'Easiest' is a superlative, wrong for comparing just two things, and 'as easy' does not fit with 'than'.

questions.prompt: Which sentence correctly compares the three product lines?
options: Product C sold the better of the three product lines.
Product C sold the best of the three product lines.
Product C sold more good than the others.
Product C is selling gooder than the others.
Product C sold the goodest of all.
questions.explanationTR: 'Best' is the correct superlative of 'well/good' for comparing three or more things. 'The better of the three' uses a comparative where a superlative is needed, and 'more good', 'gooder', and 'goodest' are not standard English forms.

questions.prompt: Attendance this month was ---- than we expected.
questions.explanationTR: Comparing the actual result with the expectation needs the comparative 'lower'. 'Lowest' is a superlative, and 'more low'/'most low' are wrong forms since 'low' takes '-er/-est'.

questions.prompt: Out of everyone on the team, she gave ---- presentation.
questions.explanationTR: 'Confident' is a longer adjective, so its superlative is 'the most confident', not '-est'. 'More confident' is a comparative, wrong for comparing everyone on the team, and 'confidentest' is not a real word.

items.definition: A short transcript of a business presentation about regional sales trends, with eight questions

passage.title: A Presentation on Regional Sales
passage.body:
Good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining today's session. My name is Elena Martins, and I lead the regional sales team. Over the next fifteen minutes, I will walk you through our latest results and explain the main trends behind the numbers.

Let's start with an overview. On this slide, you can see sales figures from our four regions: North, South, East, and West. As the chart shows, the North region had the highest growth this year, with a steady rise every quarter. The South region also performed well, though its growth was more gradual than the North's.

The East region tells a different story. Sales there rose sharply in the first quarter, then fell just as quickly in the second. This kind of fluctuation usually points to a single large order rather than a genuine change in demand, and our data supports that idea. By the third quarter, East had returned to a level similar to last year's.

The West region had the smallest increase of the four, but it was still positive, and the team there deserves credit for a difficult market.

I want to highlight one more point before we move on. When we compare this year with last year, overall growth was significantly higher, and customer satisfaction scores were also better across every region. That is the clearest sign that our new approach is working.

Now, let's look more closely at what made the North region so successful, and what the other regions can learn from it. I will keep this next part brief, because I know you are waiting for the question and answer session at the end, and I promise we will have plenty of time for that.

questions.prompt: Which region had the highest growth this year, according to the speaker?
questions.explanationTR: The speaker says the North region had the highest growth this year, with a steady rise every quarter. No other region is described as having faster growth.

questions.prompt: How did the South region's growth compare with the North's?
options: It was faster than the North's
It was more gradual than the North's
It was exactly the same as the North's
It declined while the North's grew
questions.explanationTR: The passage says the South region's growth 'was more gradual than the North's', meaning slower and steadier, not faster or equal.

questions.prompt: What most likely explains the East region's pattern of a sharp rise followed by a sharp fall?
options: A mistake in the sales data
A single large order rather than a real change in demand
A permanent decline in the market
A new competitor entering the region
questions.explanationTR: The passage explains that this kind of fluctuation 'usually points to a single large order rather than a genuine change in demand.' There is no mention of a data mistake, a permanent decline, or a new competitor.

questions.prompt: How does the passage describe the West region's result?
options: The largest increase of the four regions
A decrease compared with last year
No change from the previous year
The smallest increase of the four, but still positive
The region with the highest customer satisfaction
questions.explanationTR: The speaker states that the West region 'had the smallest increase of the four, but it was still positive,' ruling out a decrease or no change at all.

questions.prompt: According to the speaker, how did this year's overall growth compare with last year's?
questions.explanationTR: The speaker directly compares this year with last year and says overall growth 'was significantly higher,' not lower or unchanged.

questions.prompt: What does the speaker say about customer satisfaction scores?
options: They were better across every region
They fell in every region except the North
They were unavailable for this year
They were the same as last year
They improved only in the North
questions.explanationTR: The passage says customer satisfaction scores 'were also better across every region,' not worse or unavailable, and not limited to one region.

questions.prompt: What will the speaker most likely talk about next?
options: The history of the sales team
What made the North region successful and what others can learn
questions.explanationTR: The speaker announces she will look at 'what made the North region so successful, and what the other regions can learn from it,' which is the clear next topic.

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker say she will keep the next part brief?
options: She is running out of slides
She has technical problems with the projector
She was asked to finish early by her manager
She wants to leave time for the question and answer session
She thinks the audience is not interested
questions.explanationTR: The speaker explains she will be brief because the audience is 'waiting for the question and answer session at the end,' and she wants to leave enough time for it.

items.definition: using if-clauses to talk about likely and unlikely outcomes in a negotiation
items.explanationTR:
In negotiations, we use conditional sentences to talk about possible outcomes and their results.

• First conditional (if + present simple, ... will + base verb): a realistic condition and its likely result.
  - If you lower the price, we will sign today.
  - If they refuse the terms, we will look for another supplier.

• Second conditional (if + past simple, ... would + base verb): an unlikely, hypothetical, or unreal condition and its result now or in the future.
  - If I were the buyer, I would ask for a longer warranty.
  - If we had a bigger budget, we would accept your first offer.

• Choose the first conditional when the condition is realistic or still open to negotiation. Choose the second conditional when the condition is unlikely, imaginary, or you want to sound more polite and less direct.

• In the second conditional, 'were' is used for all subjects after 'if' in careful, formal English: If I were you, I would negotiate harder.

• Both types use a comma when the if-clause comes first, but no comma when it comes second: We will sign today if you lower the price.

questions.prompt: If you ---- us a ten percent discount, we will sign the contract today.
questions.explanationTR: The first conditional needs the present simple after 'if' for a realistic condition; 'will sign' in the main clause confirms this is a first conditional sentence.

questions.prompt: If I ---- you, I would ask for a longer payment period.
questions.explanationTR: This is a hypothetical second conditional, so the if-clause uses the past simple, and 'were' is the standard form for all subjects; 'am' is present tense and does not fit the unreal, hypothetical situation.

questions.prompt: We ---- the deal if they don't meet our minimum price.
questions.explanationTR: The if-clause uses the present simple ('don't meet'), so this is a first conditional and the main clause needs 'will' plus the base verb; 'would not sign' wrongly shifts to the second conditional pattern.

questions.prompt: If the supplier ---- more flexible, we would consider a longer contract.
questions.explanationTR: 'Would consider' in the main clause signals a second conditional, so the if-clause needs the past form 'were', not the present tense 'is', which would suggest a first conditional instead.

questions.prompt: ---- , they will lose the contract.
options: If they didn't lower their price
If they will not lower their price
If they wouldn't lower their price
If they not lower their price
If they don't lower their price
questions.explanationTR: 'Will lose' in the main clause shows a first conditional, so the if-clause must use the present simple 'don't lower'; the other options wrongly use past forms or 'will' inside the if-clause.

questions.prompt: If we had more leverage, we ---- for a better deal.
questions.explanationTR: The if-clause 'had more leverage' is a past-simple hypothetical, so the main clause needs 'would' plus the base verb 'push'; 'will push' incorrectly mixes in the first conditional pattern.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that correctly uses the first conditional.
options: If you signed today, we will include free installation.

lessons.title: Grammar: Present perfect vs past simple for results

items.headword: Present perfect vs past simple for results
items.definition: choosing between present perfect and past simple when reporting business results
items.explanationTR:
When we report business and financial results, we choose between the present perfect and the past simple depending on whether the time is finished or still connected to now.

• Present perfect (have/has + past participle): used when there's no finished time reference, or when a period such as 'this year' or 'so far' is still going on. It connects a past event to a present result.
  - Revenue has grown by ten percent this year.
  - The company has not published its results yet.

• Past simple: used with a finished time reference, such as 'last quarter,' 'in 2023,' or 'yesterday.'
  - Revenue grew by ten percent last quarter.
  - The company published its results in March.

• Time words are the clue: 'so far,' 'this year,' 'yet,' and 'already' usually go with the present perfect; 'last year,' 'in 2022,' and 'yesterday' go with the past simple.

• In a quarterly report, both forms often appear together: 'Earnings have improved since April, although they fell sharply in March.'

questions.prompt: Revenue ---- by fifteen percent so far this year.
questions.explanationTR: 'So far this year' describes an unfinished period connected to now, which needs the present perfect 'has grown'; the simple past 'grew' would require a finished time reference instead.

questions.prompt: The company ---- its earnings report last Tuesday.
questions.explanationTR: 'Last Tuesday' is a finished, dated time reference, so the past simple 'published' is required; the present perfect 'has published' is not used with a specific finished time like this.

questions.prompt: We ---- the new budget yet; the decision comes tomorrow.
questions.explanationTR: 'Yet' signals the present perfect in negative sentences about something that has not happened up to now ('haven't approved'); 'hadn't approved' refers to a time before another past event, and 'not approved' is missing its auxiliary verb.

questions.prompt: Profits ---- sharply in 2022, before recovering the following year.
questions.explanationTR: 'In 2022' is a specific, finished time reference, so the past simple 'fell' is correct; the present perfect 'have fallen' is not used with a dated past time like this.

questions.prompt: So far this quarter, the company ---- three new contracts.
questions.explanationTR: 'So far this quarter' describes a period that is still ongoing, so the present perfect 'has signed' is needed; 'signed' would wrongly treat the quarter as already finished.

questions.prompt: Turnover ---- significantly since the new product launched, according to the latest figures.
questions.explanationTR: 'Since' connects a past starting point to the present, which is a classic present perfect trigger ('has increased'); the simple past 'increased' does not fit with 'since' in this way.

questions.prompt: Choose the sentence that correctly reports a finished, dated result.
options: The board has approved the budget last month.
The board approved the budget last month.
The board have approved the budget last month.
The board was approving the budget last month.
The board approves the budget last month.
questions.explanationTR: 'Last month' is a finished, dated time reference, so the past simple 'approved' is correct; the present perfect forms 'has/have approved' cannot be combined with a specific finished time like 'last month', 'was approving' describes an activity in progress rather than a result, and 'approves' is present tense.

questions.explanationTR: 'Over the past six months' plus 'are still rising' shows an unfinished period connected to now, which needs the present perfect 'have risen'; the simple past 'rose' would suggest the rise is already over.

passage.title: Quarterly Report: Solara Bikes, Q2
passage.body:
Solara Bikes has published its results for the second quarter of the fiscal year. Revenue reached eighteen million dollars, an increase of nine percent year-on-year. Much of this growth came from strong demand in the electric bicycle line, which now makes up almost half of total turnover.

Despite the rise in revenue, net income fell slightly compared to the same quarter last year. Overhead costs, especially shipping and warehouse rent, increased faster than expected, and the company had to write off a batch of damaged inventory. Expenses for the quarter reached eleven million dollars, leaving a smaller profit margin than shareholders had hoped for.

The balance sheet remains healthy. Total assets grew to sixty million dollars, while liabilities stayed roughly the same, so shareholder equity improved. Cash flow was also positive: the finance team collected outstanding invoices more quickly, which helped the company avoid a cash shortage during a slow month.

Looking ahead, management issued a cautious forecast for the third quarter. They expect the new factory to break even within a year, and they do not plan to raise the dividend until earnings recover fully. An external audit is scheduled for next month to confirm the figures in this report before they are shared with investors.

Overall, the quarter showed healthy growth in sales but a small decline in net income. The board believes the company is still on track to meet its full-year targets, as long as overhead costs are brought under control before the next fiscal year begins.

items.definition: how to use the passive voice to describe processes, results and reports without naming who did the action
items.explanationTR:
In business reports, writers often use the passive voice to focus on an action or result rather than on who performed it. This is common when the person responsible is unknown, unimportant, or already clear from the situation.

Form the passive with a form of "be" plus the past participle:
• Present simple passive: The product is tested before release.
• Past simple passive: The campaign was launched in March.
• Present perfect passive: The results have been reviewed by the team.
• Future simple passive: The new packaging will be introduced next season.
• Past perfect passive: The survey had been completed before the launch date.

Add "by + agent" only when the agent matters:
• The rebranding was designed by an outside agency.

In marketing and business writing, the passive keeps attention on products, customers, and results rather than on the writer's own team:
• Customer feedback is collected after every purchase.
• Over a thousand coupons were redeemed last month.

Don't overuse the passive, though. When the person or thing performing the action is the point of the sentence, the active voice is clearer and more natural.

questions.prompt: Customer feedback ---- after every purchase.
questions.explanationTR: Routine, repeated actions with an unstated subject take the present simple passive (is collected); "collects" and "has collected" are active forms that would need a stated subject performing the action.

questions.prompt: The new marketing campaign ---- last month.
questions.explanationTR: The finished time marker "last month" needs the past simple, and the campaign receives the action, so the passive "was launched" is correct; "has been launched" is present perfect, which cannot be used with a finished time like "last month."

questions.prompt: Over one thousand coupons ---- since the sale began.
questions.explanationTR: "Since the sale began" signals an action continuing up to now, so the present perfect passive "have been redeemed" is needed, agreeing with the plural subject "coupons"; the future perfect "will have been redeemed" describes a later deadline, not the present result.

questions.prompt: The rebranding ---- by an outside design agency.
questions.explanationTR: Because the agent ("an outside design agency") is stated and important, the passive "was designed" is used with "by"; "is designing" would wrongly make the rebranding itself the one doing the designing.

questions.prompt: Starting next year, the product ---- to every retailer in the region.
questions.explanationTR: "Starting next year" points to the future, and the product receives the action, so the future passive "will be distributed" is correct; "will distribute" is active and would mean the product itself does the distributing, and "would have been distributed" is a conditional form that does not fit a real future plan.

questions.prompt: The market research ---- before the launch date was even set.
questions.explanationTR: The research finished before another past event ("the launch date was even set"), so the past perfect passive "had been completed" is needed; the present perfect "has been completed" would place the action too close to now.

questions.prompt: The survey results ---- in the company newsletter last week.
questions.explanationTR: "Results" is plural, so it needs the plural passive "were published"; "was published" wrongly treats "results" as singular, and "had been publishing" is an unnecessary, unnatural aspect here.

questions.prompt: An outside agency ---- the new slogan for last year's campaign.
questions.explanationTR: Here "an outside agency" is the subject performing the action, so the active "created" is correct; using a passive form would incorrectly turn the agency into the receiver of the action.

questions.explanationTR: Packaging is the material and design that wraps a product, which is what a design team works on so that it stands out on shelves; distribution is the process of getting products to stores, not something that is seen on a shelf.

questions.prompt: Marketers chose teenagers and young adults as the ---- for the campaign.
questions.explanationTR: The target audience is the specific group a campaign is aimed at, which fits choosing teenagers and young adults; market share refers to a company's percentage of total sales, not a group of people.

questions.prompt: To reach that group quickly, the brand hired a well-known ---- to post about the drink online.
questions.explanationTR: An influencer is a person with online followers who is paid to promote products, matching someone hired to post online; a sponsor typically funds an event rather than posting personal content.

questions.prompt: The company opened its first flagship ---- in the capital, complete with tasting stations.
questions.explanationTR: An outlet is a single store location, which fits a "flagship" opening in one city; a retailer refers more generally to a selling business, not one specific store.

questions.prompt: Within a month, most major ---- were stocking the drink in their stores nationwide.
questions.explanationTR: Retailers are businesses that sell products to customers in stores, so they are the ones who stock the drink; competitors make or sell rival products and would not stock it, and the other options are not businesses at all.

questions.prompt: Even without more advertising, satisfied customers kept telling their friends about the drink, proof of the power of ----.
questions.explanationTR: Word of mouth describes information passed between people without advertising, matching customers telling their friends; a testimonial is a formal written or spoken statement, not casual conversation.

questions.prompt: A year later, the brand introduced a rewards card to build customer ---- and encourage repeat purchases.
questions.explanationTR: Customer loyalty is the ongoing support of a brand, which fits a rewards card aimed at repeat purchases; feedback is comments about a product, not the ongoing relationship a loyalty card targets.

lessons.title: Grammar: Future forms for plans and deadlines

items.headword: future forms for plans and deadlines
items.definition: how to talk about plans, arrangements and deadlines using will, going to, present continuous and the future perfect
items.explanationTR:
English uses different future forms depending on how fixed or certain a plan is.

• Present continuous for fixed arrangements: The designers are presenting the prototype on Thursday.
• "Going to" for intentions and evidence-based predictions: We're going to miss the deadline unless we get more help.
• Will for decisions made at the moment of speaking, offers and promises, and predictions based on opinion (often with I think or probably): I'll send the deliverable by Friday.
• Future perfect for an action completed before a future deadline: By June, she will have finished her internship.
• Future continuous for an action in progress at a specific future time: This time next week, the team will be rolling out the update.

Use "going to" when a plan or decision already exists, and "will" when you decide at the moment of speaking. Use the future perfect specifically to talk about deadlines: something that will already be done by a certain point in time. Often more than one form is possible, so choose the one that matches what you mean.

In project and career contexts, choosing the right future form makes timelines and commitments clear to teammates and clients.

questions.prompt: We ---- the new feature next Monday. It's already on the calendar.
questions.explanationTR: A fixed arrangement already on the calendar is naturally expressed with the present continuous (are launching); "launched," "have launched" and "were launching" refer to the past and clash with "next Monday," and "are going to launching" is not a grammatical form.

questions.prompt: Look at how much work is still left on the list. We ---- the deadline.
questions.explanationTR: A prediction based on present evidence (the work still left on the list) uses "going to" (are going to miss); "will have been missing" wrongly adds a continuous aspect to a simple prediction.

questions.prompt: You look really busy. Leave the slides to me — I ---- them tomorrow morning.
questions.explanationTR: An offer made at the moment of speaking uses "will" (I'll prepare / will prepare); "prepared" and "have prepared" refer to the past and clash with "tomorrow morning," and "would prepare" is a conditional form with no condition.

questions.prompt: By the end of the month, she ---- her internship.
questions.explanationTR: The future perfect (will have finished) shows an action completed before a stated future deadline ("by the end of the month"); "has finished," "finished" and "had finished" look back from the present or the past, not from a point in the future.

questions.prompt: This time next week, the whole team ---- on the new rollout.
questions.explanationTR: The future continuous (will be working) describes an action in progress at a specific future moment ("this time next week"); the simple future (will work) does not capture that ongoing sense.

questions.prompt:
A: Sam has just finished his own work for today.
B: Oh, good. In that case, I ---- the report to him.
questions.explanationTR: B decides at the moment of speaking, after hearing the news ("In that case"), so "will" is used (I'll delegate / will delegate); "delegated" and "have delegated" describe something already done, and "would delegate" needs a condition.

questions.prompt: It's confirmed: we ---- the prototype to the client at 10 a.m. tomorrow.
questions.explanationTR: A confirmed arrangement with a specific time ("10 a.m. tomorrow") is naturally expressed with the present continuous (are presenting); the past forms clash with "tomorrow," and "are going to presenting" is not a grammatical form.

questions.prompt: Please don't call Kenji between 2 and 4 p.m. tomorrow — he ---- the client workshop then.
questions.explanationTR: An action in progress during a specific future period ("between 2 and 4 p.m. tomorrow") uses the future continuous (will be running); "will have run" would mean the workshop is already over by then, and the other options refer to the past.

items.definition: An update email to a project team and seven questions about it

passage.title: A Project Update
passage.body:
Dear team,

Here is a short update on where the mobile app project stands. We are two weeks away from the final deadline, and most of the milestones on our timeline have already been reached. The design deliverable was approved last week, and the development team is now testing the last few features before the rollout.

There was one bottleneck in July, when the testing team had to wait for feedback from stakeholders before continuing. Once that feedback arrived, the workflow returned to normal, and we managed to catch up within a few days. To keep the project on track, our project manager decided to delegate two smaller tasks to team members with lighter workloads.

The scope of the project has stayed close to the original plan, with only minor changes to the settings screen. Everyone has worked hard, and the extra effort has not gone unnoticed. In fact, our project manager mentioned that Dana, who joined the team as an intern last year, will likely receive a promotion once the rollout is complete. Her mentor, Farah, says Dana's growing skill set made her the obvious choice.

Our next progress report will go out after the rollout, once we can share real results from users. Until then, please continue sending any concerns to your team lead so we can address them before the deadline.

Thank you all for your hard work this month.

Best,
Priya

questions.prompt: According to the update, how close is the team to the final deadline?
questions.explanationTR: Priya writes that the team is "two weeks away from the final deadline"; the other options do not match the timeframe stated in the update.

questions.prompt: What caused the bottleneck mentioned in the update?
options: A delay in feedback from stakeholders
A sudden change in project scope
A problem with the testing software
questions.explanationTR: The update says the team "had to wait for feedback from stakeholders before continuing"; the other causes are never mentioned as the source of the delay.

questions.prompt: What did the project manager do to keep the project on track after the bottleneck?
options: The scope of the project was reduced
Two tasks were delegated to team members with lighter workloads
A new, more experienced project manager was brought in to take over the schedule
The rollout was canceled for the month
questions.explanationTR: The update states the project manager "decided to delegate two smaller tasks to team members with lighter workloads"; the passage never mentions extending the deadline or hiring anyone new.

questions.prompt: What is expected to happen to Dana after the rollout?
options: She will resign from the company
She will take a probation period
She will likely receive a promotion
She will be given a smaller workload
questions.explanationTR: The update says Dana "will likely receive a promotion once the rollout is complete"; Farah is described as Dana's mentor, not the other way around.

questions.prompt: Based on the update, when will the next progress report be sent?
options: Right when the bottleneck first appeared, before it was even resolved
As soon as the scope changed
At the very start of the project
After the rollout, once results from users are available
questions.explanationTR: Priya writes that the "next progress report will go out after the rollout, once we can share real results from users"; no fixed weekly schedule is mentioned in the update.

questions.prompt: How has the project's scope changed compared to the original plan?
options: It has stayed close to the original plan, with only minor changes
It expanded to include several new features
It was cut in half to save time
It changed completely once the stakeholders asked for a much larger set of features than planned
It was replaced by a completely different plan
questions.explanationTR: The update says the scope "has stayed close to the original plan, with only minor changes to the settings screen"; no major expansion or replacement is described.

questions.prompt: According to Farah, why is Dana the obvious choice for a promotion?
questions.explanationTR: The update says that Farah, Dana's mentor, believes "Dana's growing skill set made her the obvious choice"; Dana joined only last year as an intern, and workloads, reports and stakeholders are mentioned in other contexts.
